about: "Say it in context" prompts for unit-2 (docs/apstat-architecture.md, "Justification trainer"; spec section 6). Written in Phase 3 from the banks; checked by checkJustify in scripts/lib/apstat-exams.mjs, numbers recomputed in JUSTIFY_NUMBERS. Invented data.

prompts.title: Define it, name it, then compute
prompts.context: A basketball player makes 30% of her three point shots. In tomorrow's game she will take 10 three point shots. Assume the shots are independent.
prompts.prompt: Calculate the probability that she makes at least 4 of the 10 shots. Show your work as the exam expects.
checklist: Defines the random variable in context: $X$ = the number of the 10 shots she makes
Names the distribution and its parameters: binomial with $n = 10$ and $p = 0.3$
Writes the event correctly with its complement: $P(X \ge 4) = 1 - P(X \le 3)$
Gives the answer, about 0.350

earns.answer: Let $X$ = the number of the 10 three point shots she makes. $X$ is binomial with $n = 10$ and $p = 0.3$. $P(X \ge 4) = 1 - P(X \le 3) = 1 - 0.6496 = 0.350$.
earns.why: It defines $X$ in context, names the distribution with both parameters, states the event and its complement, and gives the value.

misses.why: Calculator syntax is not work: the random variable is never defined, the distribution and parameters are not named in words, and the event $X \ge 4$ is never stated.

prompts.title: Tie the probability to the claim
prompts.context: A delivery company claims that 80% of its packages arrive on time. A customer tracks a random sample of 20 of its packages and finds that only 12 arrive on time. If the claim is true, the probability that 12 or fewer of 20 packages arrive on time is about 0.032.
prompts.prompt: Explain whether the customer's result gives reason to doubt the company's claim.
checklist: States the probability as conditional on the claim: if 80% arrive on time, 12 or fewer of 20 happens with probability about 0.032
Judges that probability as small (unusual): this result would rarely happen by chance if the claim were true
Concludes in context: the result gives reason to doubt that 80% of the company's packages arrive on time

earns.answer: If the company's claim is true, the probability that 12 or fewer of 20 randomly chosen packages arrive on time is only about 0.032. A result this low would happen by chance only about 3 times in 100 samples, so it is unusual. The customer's result gives reason to doubt the claim that 80% of the company's packages arrive on time.
earns.why: It conditions the probability on the claim, judges it as small, and draws the conclusion about the claim in context.

misses.answer: The probability is 0.032, so the company is lying and fewer than 80% arrive on time.
misses.why: It never says the probability assumes the claim is true, and a small probability gives reason to doubt a claim; it does not prove the company is lying.

prompts.title: Which way does the condition go?
prompts.context: Of the 500 students at a school, 120 play a sport and 80 are in the band; 20 students do both. A student says, "The probability that a band member plays a sport is the same as the probability that an athlete is in the band."
prompts.prompt: Explain whether the student is right, using the two conditional probabilities.
checklist: Computes $P(\text{sport} \mid \text{band}) = \frac{20}{80} = 0.25$
Computes $P(\text{band} \mid \text{sport}) = \frac{20}{120} \approx 0.167$
Concludes the student is wrong: the conditional probabilities differ because the groups being conditioned on have different sizes

earns.answer: The student is wrong. $P(\text{sport} \mid \text{band}) = \frac{20}{80} = 0.25$, but $P(\text{band} \mid \text{sport}) = \frac{20}{120} \approx 0.167$. Both use the same 20 students who do both, but the first divides by the 80 band members and the second by the 120 athletes, so the probabilities differ.
earns.why: It computes both conditional probabilities, compares them, and explains why reversing the condition changes the denominator.

misses.answer: The student is right, because 20 students are in both groups either way.
misses.why: The overlap is the same, but a conditional probability divides by the group in the condition; the answer never computes either probability.

prompts.title: Show that two events are not independent
prompts.context: In a town, 40% of households own a dog, 25% own a cat, and 15% own both a dog and a cat. One household is chosen at random.
prompts.prompt: Determine whether owning a dog and owning a cat are independent events. Justify your answer with probabilities.
checklist: States the check: independent if $P(\text{dog} \cap \text{cat}) = P(\text{dog}) \cdot P(\text{cat})$ (or $P(\text{cat} \mid \text{dog}) = P(\text{cat})$)
Computes $P(\text{dog}) \cdot P(\text{cat}) = 0.40(0.25) = 0.10$ and compares it with 0.15 (or $P(\text{cat} \mid \text{dog}) = 0.375$ with 0.25)
Concludes the events are not independent because the values differ

earns.answer: If the events were independent, $P(\text{dog} \cap \text{cat})$ would equal $P(\text{dog}) \cdot P(\text{cat}) = 0.40(0.25) = 0.10$. But $P(\text{dog} \cap \text{cat}) = 0.15$, which is not 0.10, so owning a dog and owning a cat are not independent. (Equivalently, $P(\text{cat} \mid \text{dog}) = \frac{0.15}{0.40} = 0.375$, not 0.25.)
earns.why: It names the rule, substitutes the numbers, and draws the conclusion from the comparison.

misses.answer: They are not independent because some households have both a dog and a cat.
misses.why: Having both is about overlap (the events are not mutually exclusive); independence is a separate check that needs the probabilities compared.

prompts.title: Normal work shown as the exam asks
prompts.context: The heights of adult women in a country are approximately normal with mean 64.5 inches and standard deviation 2.5 inches.
prompts.prompt: Calculate the proportion of the country's adult women who are taller than 68 inches. Show your work.
checklist: Names the distribution and its parameters: normal with mean 64.5 inches and standard deviation 2.5 inches
Gives the boundary and direction: the area to the right of 68 inches (a labeled sketch or $P(\text{height} > 68)$)
Standardizes or names the technology input: $z = \frac{68 - 64.5}{2.5} = 1.40$
Gives the answer: about 0.081

earns.answer: Heights are normal with mean 64.5 inches and standard deviation 2.5 inches. We want $P(\text{height} > 68)$, the area to the right of 68. $z = \frac{68 - 64.5}{2.5} = 1.40$, and the area to the right of $z = 1.40$ is $1 - 0.9192 = 0.0808$. About 8.1% of the country's adult women are taller than 68 inches.
earns.why: It names the distribution, the parameters, the boundary and the direction, then shows the standardization and the answer in context.

misses.why: Calculator syntax alone is not accepted as work: the distribution, the parameters and the region must be labeled in words or a sketch.

prompts.title: Read a simulation as evidence
prompts.context: A teacher claims a quiz's 10 true or false questions have random answers, so a student guessing on every question would get each one right with probability 0.5. A student who says he guessed got 9 right. The teacher simulates 200 guessers; 7 of the 200 simulated guessers got 9 or more right.
prompts.prompt: Explain what the simulation says about the student's claim that he guessed.
checklist: Estimates the probability from the simulation: about $\frac{7}{200} = 0.035$
Interprets it conditionally: if the student were guessing, 9 or more right would happen in only about 3.5% of trials
Concludes in context: this is unusual, so the simulation gives evidence against the claim that he guessed (it does not prove he did not)

earns.answer: In the simulation, 7 of 200 guessers got 9 or more right, so the estimated probability is $\frac{7}{200} = 0.035$. If the student were really guessing, a score of 9 or more would happen only about 3.5% of the time, which is unusual. So the simulation gives evidence against the student's claim that he guessed on every question.
earns.why: It counts the trials at or beyond the observed result, interprets the estimate assuming the claim, and draws a careful conclusion.

misses.answer: Most simulated guessers got around 5 right, so the student was not guessing.
misses.why: It never uses the count of trials with 9 or more, gives no probability, and states the conclusion as certain.
